title: Hammerhead shark
wiki_lead:
The hammerhead sharks are a group of sharks that form the family Sphyrnidae, named for the unusual and distinctive form of their heads, which are flattened and laterally extended into a cephalofoil (a T-shape or "hammer"). The shark's eyes are placed one on each end of this T-shaped structure, with their small mouths directly centered and underneath. Most hammerhead species are placed in the genus Sphyrna, while the winghead shark is placed in its own genus, Eusphyra. Many different—but not necessarily mutually exclusive—functions have been postulated for the cephalofoil, including sensory reception, manoeuvering, and prey manipulation. The cephalofoil gives the shark superior binocular vision and depth perception, as well as increased surface area for electroreceptors.
Hammerheads are found worldwide, preferring life in warmer waters along coastlines and continental shelves. Unlike most sharks, some hammerhead species will congregate and swim in large schools during the day, becoming solitary hunters at night.

The hammerhead sharks are a group of sharks that form the family Sphyrnidae, named for the unusual and distinctive form of their heads, which are flattened and laterally extended into a cephalofoil (a T-shape or "hammer"). The shark's eyes are placed one on each end of this T-shaped structure, with their small mouths directly centered and underneath. Most hammerhead species are placed in the genus Sphyrna, while the winghead shark is placed in its own genus, Eusphyra. Many different—but not necessarily mutually exclusive—functions have been postulated for the cephalofoil, including sensory reception, manoeuvering, and prey manipulation. The cephalofoil gives the shark superior binocular vision and depth perception, as well as increased surface area for electroreceptors.
Hammerheads are found worldwide, preferring life in warmer waters along coastlines and continental shelves. Unlike most sharks, some hammerhead species will congregate and swim in large schools during the day, becoming solitary hunters at night.


Description

Hammerhead shark species vary in length and weight. The largest species, the great hammerhead, has an average length of 13.1 feet (4.0 m) and weight of 500 pounds (230 kg). The smallest species, the bonnethead shark, can reach 5 feet (1,5 m) in length and 24 pounds (10,8 kg) in weight. One specimen caught off the Florida coast in 1906 weighed over 680 kg (1,500 lb). They are usually light gray and have a greenish tint. Their bellies are white, which allows them to blend into the background when viewed from below and sneak up to their prey. Their heads have lateral projections that give them a hammer-like shape. While overall similar, this shape differs somewhat between species; examples are: a distinct T-shape in the great hammerhead, a rounded head with a central notch in the scalloped hammerhead, and an unnotched rounded head in the smooth hammerhead.
Hammerheads have disproportionately small mouths compared to other shark species. Some species are also known to form schools. In the evening, like most other sharks, they become solitary hunters. National Geographic explained that hammerheads can be found in warm, tropical waters, but during the summer, they begin a mass migration period in search of colder waters.


Taxonomy and evolution
Because sharks do not have mineralized bones and rarely fossilize, only their teeth are commonly found as fossils. Their closest relatives are the requiem sharks (Carcharinidae). Based on a recent combined molecular and paleontological study, the ancestor of the hammerheads probably lived in the Cretaceous or Paleocene. Definitive fossils of the family date back to the Eocene. Prior DNA studies had estimated the family to have arisen in the Miocene, about 20 million years ago.
Using mitochondrial DNA, a phylogenetic tree of the hammerhead sharks showed the winghead shark as sister to the rest of the hammerhead sharks. As the winghead shark has proportionately the largest "hammer" of the hammerhead sharks, this suggests that the first ancestral hammerhead sharks also had large hammers.


Cephalofoil

The hammer-like shape of the head may have evolved at least in part to enhance the animal's vision. The positioning of the eyes, mounted on the sides of the shark's distinctive hammer head, allows 360° of vision in the vertical plane, meaning the animals can see above and below them at all times. They also have an increased binocular vision and depth of visual field as a result of the cephalofoil.
The shape of the head was previously thought to aid in close-quarters maneuverability, allowing sharp turning movement without losing stability. However, the unusual structure of its vertebrae instead has been found to be instrumental in making the turns correctly, more so than the shape of its head (though it would also shift and provide lift).

grok_lead: Hammerhead sharks comprise the family Sphyrnidae within the order Carcharhiniformes, consisting of ten extant species distinguished by their cephalofoil, a flattened and transversely expanded head morphology that repositions sensory structures such as eyes, nostrils, and ampullae of Lorenzini to improve binocular vision, olfactory acuity, and electroreceptive prey localization. This adaptation also confers hydrodynamic advantages, including reduced fluid moments during turns and enhanced maneuverability for capturing agile prey. The species vary markedly in cephalofoil shape, from the narrowly rounded form in the bonnethead ( Sphyrna tiburo) to the broadly mallet-like extension in the great hammerhead ( Sphyrna mokarran). These sharks inhabit primarily tropical and subtropical marine environments, favoring coastal and continental shelf waters where they hunt bottom-associated prey such as stingrays, crustaceans, and teleost fishes, though larger individuals also consume smaller sharks and pelagic species. Ranging from the diminutive bonnethead, which attains a maximum length of approximately 1.5 meters, to the great hammerhead exceeding 6 meters, hammerheads exhibit viviparous reproduction with females producing litters of 6 to 55 pups depending on species and size. Their global distribution spans the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans, with some populations demonstrating seasonal migrations between nursery grounds and foraging areas. Conservation assessments by the International Union for Conservation of Nature classify most hammerhead species as threatened, with the great hammerhead and scalloped hammerhead ( Sphyrna lewini) rated as critically endangered due to intense fishing pressure for their valuable fins, high post-capture mortality, and slow population recovery rates stemming from late maturity and low fecundity. Regulatory measures, including listings under the Endangered Species Act for certain populations and CITES Appendix II protections, aim to curb international trade, though enforcement challenges and bycatch persist as primary threats.
